5610: Several passages in the Hebrew Bible picture God presiding over a heavenly assembly of lesser spiritual beings, called "sons of God", "holy ones" or even "gods" (elohim). Psalm 82 is the clearest example: God stands up in "the divine council" and judges the gods who have ruled the nations unjustly. Many scholars, including the late Michael Heiser, think this "divine council" idea is a key to reading the whole Bible story, from Babel and the scattering of the nations to Pentecost and the nations healed in Revelation. Others agree the council imagery is real but read some of the key texts differently: "let us" in Genesis 1:26 as a hint of the Trinity or a plural of majesty, the "gods" of Psalm 82 as human judges, and the "sons of God" of Genesis 6 as godly men from Seth's line. Critical historians such as Mark Smith see the council as a leftover from an older Israelite religion that only slowly became monotheistic. All of these readings agree on one thing the texts state plainly: in the Bible, Yahweh alone is Creator, has no equal, and is the only one to be worshipped.
5611: "Elohim" (usually translated "God" or "gods") is used in the Hebrew Bible for the God of Israel, for foreign gods, for members of God's heavenly assembly and once even for the ghost of Samuel, so the word alone does not tell you which being is meant.
5612: Psalm 82, 1 Kings 22, Job 1–2, Isaiah 6, Psalm 89 and Daniel 7 all describe God surrounded by a heavenly court; this much is widely agreed, since the imagery has close parallels in the Ugaritic texts about El's assembly (found from 1929).
5613: Deuteronomy 32:8 is a famous text-critical puzzle: the traditional Hebrew text says the nations were divided by the number of "the sons of Israel", but a Dead Sea Scroll and the Greek Septuagint point to "the sons of God"; many modern versions now follow the older reading.
5614: On the divine-council reading, the Bible tells a story of three rebellions (Eden, Genesis 6 and Babel), after which the nations were handed over to lesser gods while Yahweh took Israel as his own portion.
5615: That reading sees the New Testament as the reclaiming of the nations: Jesus disarms the "rulers and authorities" (Col 2:15), Pentecost reverses Babel (Acts 2) and Revelation ends with every nation worshipping the Lamb.
5616: Critics accept parts of the picture but question others: whether "let us" means a council, whether Psalm 82's "gods" are angels or human judges, whether Genesis 6 speaks of angels, and whether Isaiah's "there is no other" denies that any other gods exist.
5617: The council members are always presented as created and subordinate: they are commanded to worship Yahweh, can be judged by him, and in Psalm 82 are told they will "die like men". Nobody in the debate thinks the Bible teaches worship of more than one God.
5618: The word "monotheism" is a modern label (17th century), so scholars argue about whether it fits ancient Israel; the real question is how to describe a faith that insists on one Creator while speaking of other heavenly beings.
5620: The God of Israel, the Creator, called Elyon ("Most High"), "God of gods and Lord of lords" and "great King above all gods". He presides over the assembly and is never one member among equals.
5622: Heavenly beings called "sons of God", "holy ones", "the host of heaven" and sometimes "gods". They are present at creation, appear before Yahweh in Job's court and, on many readings, are the "gods" judged in Psalm 82.
5624: "Messengers": the Hebrew mal'ak, like the Greek angelos, describes a job rather than a kind of being, and is also used of human messengers. Examples are the visitors to Abraham, the angels on Jacob's ladder, Gabriel and Michael.
5625: Throne attendants: cherubim, seraphim, living creatures
5626: Composite guardian beings around God's throne: cherubim guarding Eden and shaped on the ark's lid, seraphim ("burning ones") in Isaiah's vision, and the four "living creatures" of Ezekiel and Revelation. Similar winged guardians flanked thrones and temples across the ancient Near East.
5628: "In the beginning God (elohim) created..." By far the commonest use: well over 2,000 of the roughly 2,600 occurrences refer to Israel's God. The form is plural but takes a singular verb here, which is why most grammarians call it a plural of majesty or "fullness" when used of Israel's God.
5630: The medium at En-dor says, "I see elohim coming up out of the earth." The ghost of a dead human is called elohim, which shows the word can mean a being from the spirit world rather than "deity" in the full sense. Heiser called it a "place of residence" term; others call it simply a broad word for supernatural beings.
5632: Jephthah tells the Ammonite king, "Will you not possess what Chemosh your god (elohim) gives you?" He argues on the other side's terms; scholars differ on whether this reflects Jephthah's real belief, diplomatic rhetoric, or simply ordinary speech about foreign gods.
5634: "God (elohim) stands in the divine council; in the midst of the gods (elohim) he holds judgment." The same word appears twice in one verse with two different referents: first the God of Israel (singular verb), then the beings he judges.
5635: The "gods" addressed as sons of the Most High
5636: "I said, 'You are gods (elohim), sons of the Most High, all of you.'" Read as heavenly beings by most modern scholars and as human judges (or Israel at Sinai) in much older Jewish and Christian interpretation. Jesus quotes this verse in John 10:34.
5638: "On all the gods (elohe) of Egypt I will execute judgments." The plagues are framed as judgment on Egypt's gods (also Num 33:4). Whether the writer means real spiritual powers, the idols and cult, or both is itself part of the debate.
5640: A slave who wants to stay is brought "to ha-elohim". The KJV and some others render "the judges"; the ESV, NRSV and most recent versions render "to God", meaning before God at the sanctuary. The "judges" reading is one support for the human-judges view of Psalm 82; many scholars think it is not needed here (compare Exod 22:8-9).
5642: Humans are made "a little lower than elohim". The Greek Septuagint and the KJV have "angels" (followed by Heb 2:7); the NRSV and NASB have "God"; the ESV has "the heavenly beings". Both are grammatically possible.
5643: The gods who must bow to Yahweh
5644: Yahweh is "God of gods (elohe ha-elohim) and Lord of lords". Compare Ps 97:7, "worship him, all you gods" (the Greek has "all his angels", quoted in Heb 1:6 by way of Deut 32:43). Council readers take these as real beings; others take them as a superlative way of saying "the supreme God".
5646: Ashtoreth (Astarte) is called the elohim of the Sidonians. Biblical Hebrew has no separate common word for "goddess", so elohim covers female deities too.
5648: The sixth day of creation, just before humans are made. Up to now God has spoken in the singular ("Let there be light").
5651: God says, "Let us make humankind in our image, after our likeness," and then the narrative says God (singular) created humankind in his image. The switch to "us" and back has puzzled readers since antiquity. Job 38:7 adds that "the sons of God" shouted for joy at the founding of the earth, so heavenly beings are imagined as present at creation.
5653: God announces his decision to the heavenly court, as kings do to their courtiers (compare 1 Kgs 22:20; Isa 6:8). He alone creates (v. 27 uses a singular verb), but humans share an "image" with the heavenly family. Held by many modern commentators, critical and conservative (Heiser among them), and anticipated by ancient Jewish interpreters such as Philo and later rabbinic readings in which God consults the angels.
5655: The plural hints at plurality within the one God: Father, Word and Spirit (the Spirit is present in Gen 1:2; John 1:3 and Col 1:16 put the Son at creation). This was the dominant reading of the Church Fathers (e.g. Irenaeus, Augustine) and the Reformers. Critics note that Hebrew readers would not have taken it this way; defenders reply that later revelation can show the fuller meaning of an earlier text.
5657: God speaks to himself, either as a royal "we" or as someone deliberating ("let's see"). Supporters point to the singular verbs around it; critics note that a royal "we" with verbs is not clearly attested in biblical Hebrew and that the "us" in Gen 3:22 ("like one of us") is hard to explain as self-talk.
5658: "Like one of us" and "Let us go down"
5659: Two more plural speeches: after the fall in Eden (Gen 3:22) and at the tower of Babel (Gen 11:7).
5662: After Adam and Eve eat, Yahweh says, "The man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil" and bars the way to the tree of life, which cherubim then guard (Gen 3:22-24). At Babel he says, "Come, let us go down and confuse their language" (Gen 11:7), scattering the peoples who then appear as the nations of Genesis 10.
5663: "One of us" means one of the heavenly beings who already know good and evil; at Babel the council acts with Yahweh, which sets up the allotting of the nations in Deut 32:8-9. Heiser treats Babel as the third great rebellion.
5664: Classical Christian readers took both as further hints of the Trinity, since in Gen 11:5 it is Yahweh who comes down.
5666: God talks to himself, as in Gen 1:26; Gen 11:7 echoes the builders' own "Come, let us" (Gen 11:3-4) as a deliberate ironic parallel, which may explain the plural without a council.
5667: The sons of God present themselves (Job)
5668: A day when "the sons of God" come to present themselves before Yahweh, like officials reporting at court (repeated in Job 2:1-7).
5672: Among the sons of God comes ha-satan, who has been roaming the earth. Yahweh points to Job's integrity; the accuser asks whether Job fears God "for nothing" and is allowed to test him within limits Yahweh sets. Job 38:7 adds that the sons of God shouted for joy at creation.
5674: A court scene: the members report and one plays a prosecutor's role. The Hebrew has the article ("the satan"), so it is probably a title, not yet a personal name; compare Zech 3:1-2. On this view the figure later identified as Satan develops from this role.
5676: The adversary is Satan himself, already fallen but still permitted access to God's court under strict control (compare Rev 12:10, "the accuser of our brothers").
5678: Many scholars treat the heavenly prologue as a literary frame that sets up the book's question (does anyone serve God for nothing?) rather than as a report of heavenly events. This is compatible with either of the above.
5679: Micaiah sees the host of heaven
5680: Kings Ahab of Israel and Jehoshaphat of Judah plan war at Ramoth-gilead; 400 prophets promise victory. The prophet Micaiah describes a vision.
5682: All the host of heaven on his right and left
5684: Yahweh asks, "Who will entice Ahab?" Members of the host offer different proposals until a spirit volunteers to be "a lying spirit" in the prophets' mouths, and Yahweh sends it. Ahab ignores the warning and dies in battle (1 Kgs 22:34-37).
5685: The clearest picture of the council deliberating: Yahweh decides the outcome, but invites proposals and delegates the means. Many critical and conservative scholars alike accept this description of the scene.
5687: Commentators wrestle with God sending a deceiving spirit. Common answers: it is judgment on a king who already rejected the truth (compare 2 Thess 2:11); Micaiah openly tells Ahab the plan, so Ahab is warned; or the vision is a dramatic way of saying God has handed Ahab over to his chosen prophets.
5689: Some, ancient and modern, read the vision as a parable Micaiah is shown rather than a literal heavenly meeting.
5691: "In the year King Uzziah died" (about 740 BC), Isaiah sees the Lord enthroned, the hem of his robe filling the temple.
5692: The Lord (Adonai) on a high throne
5694: Isaiah cries that he is lost, a man of unclean lips; a seraph touches his lips with a coal from the altar. The Lord asks, "Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?" Isaiah answers, "Here am I; send me" and receives his commission.
5696: Like Micaiah's vision, a prophet stands in the council and hears its decision; "for us" refers to the court. Jeremiah later says false prophets have not "stood in the council (sod) of Yahweh" (Jer 23:18, 22), which suggests that a true prophet's call meant access to this court.
5697: John 12:41 says Isaiah "saw his glory" (Christ's), and Acts 28:25 attributes the words to the Holy Spirit; many Fathers and Reformers took "us" as Trinitarian.
5699: The plural is a royal or deliberative form, as some explain Gen 1:26.
5701: A taunt song against the king of Babylon (Isa 14:4), full of mythic language.
5702: The "Day Star, son of Dawn" (Helel ben Shachar)
5705: The arrogant figure says, "I will ascend to heaven; above the stars of God I will set my throne on high; I will sit on the mount of assembly in the far reaches of the north (Zaphon)... I will make myself like the Most High" (Isa 14:13-14). Instead he is brought down to Sheol.
5706: Mythic background used for a human king
5707: Most commentators see a Canaanite-style myth (a lesser star-god trying to climb to the top of the divine mountain; Zaphon was Baal's mountain in the Ugaritic texts) used to mock the Babylonian king. The "mount of assembly" is the place where the council meets.
5709: From Origen and Tertullian on, many Christians read the passage as also describing Satan's fall (the Latin "Lucifer" comes from the Vulgate's rendering of "Day Star"), often linking it with Luke 10:18. Critics reply that the text names the king of Babylon; defenders argue the language goes beyond any human king.
5710: Heiser and others take the human king to be described in terms of a rebellious divine being, so the passage is about both levels at once, as in Ezek 28.
5712: A psalm of Asaph set in "the divine council" (Hebrew adat-el, "the assembly of El"), a phrase with close Ugaritic parallels.
5715: God accuses the gods of judging unjustly and favouring the wicked instead of defending the weak, the fatherless and the poor. Because of this, "the foundations of the earth are shaken." He declares, "You are gods, sons of the Most High, all of you; nevertheless, like men you shall die." The psalmist ends: "Arise, O God, judge the earth; for you shall inherit all the nations."
5717: The gods are heavenly beings set over the nations (connecting to Deut 32:8-9) who have failed; God sentences them to mortality and the psalm prays that he will take the nations back. This is the majority view of modern critical scholars (e.g. Hans-Joachim Kraus, Marvin Tate) and central to Heiser's reading.
5719: The "gods" are Israel's judges, called elohim because they judge on God's behalf (compare Exod 22:28; 2 Chr 19:6). This was common in older rabbinic and Christian interpretation (e.g. Calvin) and is still held by some evangelical scholars, who note the moral charges are about human courts and that "die like men" can mean "die like ordinary people".
5721: Some rabbinic texts read the psalm as addressed to Israel, who became "gods" (immortal) on receiving the law but lost that status through the golden calf. Some scholars think this reading lies behind John 10:34-36.
5722: The assembly of the holy ones
5723: A royal psalm praising God's faithfulness to David's line.
5727: The heavens praise Yahweh's wonders "in the assembly of the holy ones". "Who in the skies can be compared to Yahweh? Who among the sons of God is like Yahweh, a God greatly feared in the council of the holy ones?"
5729: Almost all interpreters accept that the holy ones are heavenly beings; the point is that none of them compares to Yahweh. Council readers stress that such a comparison only makes sense if the others are real.
5731: Some read the heavenly assembly here as poetic praise language (the heavens themselves praising) rather than evidence for a structured council.
5732: The Ancient of Days and the Son of Man
5733: Daniel's vision of four beasts rising from the sea, representing successive empires.
5737: One like a son of man
5738: Thrones are set in place (plural), the Ancient of Days sits, "the court sat in judgment, and the books were opened." The beasts are judged. Then one "like a son of man" comes with the clouds of heaven and receives everlasting dominion over all peoples, nations and languages. Daniel elsewhere calls heavenly beings "watchers" and "holy ones" who issue decrees (Dan 4:17).
5740: Jesus applies the scene to himself at his trial (Mark 14:62), and the early church read the son of man as Christ, who receives the nations' dominion. This is the classical Christian reading.
5742: The interpretation in the chapter links the kingdom to "the people of the saints of the Most High" (Dan 7:27), so many scholars think the figure represents faithful Israel, or Israel's angelic patron Michael (John J. Collins argues for an angelic figure).
5743: The plural thrones show a court; the riding on clouds is language elsewhere used of Yahweh (Ps 104:3), so the son of man is a second divine figure. Heiser and others argue this "two powers" pattern prepares for the New Testament's divine Christ.
5744: The morning stars sing at creation
5745: God's speech from the whirlwind, answering Job.
5748: God asks Job where he was when the earth's foundations were laid, "when the morning stars sang together and all the sons of God shouted for joy." The heavenly beings are witnesses to creation, not helpers in it.
5749: The sons of God existed before the earth and were present when it was made, which council readers link to the "us" of Gen 1:26.
5751: Stars and sons of God are parallel, so some read it as poetic praise by the heavens (as in Ps 148:2-3), not a description of a council. Ancient readers widely linked stars and angels (compare Rev 1:20).
5752: The throne room and the Lamb
5753: John is called up through an open door in heaven and sees the throne of God.
5754: The One seated on the throne
5759: The elders and living creatures worship the Creator. No one can open the sealed scroll until the Lamb, the Lion of Judah, takes it. They sing that by his blood he ransomed people "from every tribe and language and people and nation" and made them a kingdom and priests who will reign on the earth. All creation worships God and the Lamb together.
5761: The council scene of Dan 7 is replayed: the thrones are now filled partly by redeemed humans (the elders), and the nations once scattered at Babel are gathered by the Lamb. Believers share Christ's throne (Rev 3:21).
5763: Most commentators (e.g. Richard Bauckham) stress that the scene places the Lamb on the divine side of the line between God and creatures, since he receives worship that angels refuse (Rev 19:10; Rev 22:8-9). The elders are variously read as angels, representatives of the twelve tribes and twelve apostles, or the whole people of God.
5764: The Masoretic Text (the standard medieval Hebrew text, as in the Leningrad Codex of about AD 1008) reads: "When the Most High gave to the nations their inheritance, when he divided mankind, he fixed the borders of the peoples according to the number of the sons of Israel (bene yisra'el)."
5765: A Hebrew manuscript from Qumran Cave 4, 4QDeut-j (4Q37, first century BC), preserves the end of the verse as "sons of God" (bny 'lwhym, bene elohim). Another small Qumran fragment (4QDeut-q) does not cover verse 8, but it does show a longer form of Deut 32:43 that also mentions heavenly beings, which supports the idea that the poem originally spoke of the heavenly host.
5766: The Greek Septuagint (third–second century BC) reads "according to the number of the angels of God" (angelon theou) in most manuscripts; a few manuscripts have "sons of God" (huion theou), which the critical Göttingen edition (J. W. Wevers) prints as the original Greek. Either way, the Greek translators were reading a Hebrew text that referred to heavenly beings, not to Israel.
5768: "according to the number of the children of Israel" (follows the Masoretic Text)
5770: "according to the number of the children of Israel" (Masoretic Text)
5772: "according to the number of the sons of Israel" (Masoretic Text)
5774: "according to the number of the sons of Israel", with a footnote giving the Dead Sea Scrolls/Septuagint reading "sons of God"
5776: "according to the number of the sons of God" (the first major English version to adopt the older reading)
5778: "according to the number of the sons of God", with a footnote noting the Masoretic "sons of Israel"
5780: "according to the number of the gods" (following the Qumran/Greek sense)
5782: "according to the number of the heavenly assembly" (following the Qumran/Greek sense, with a long note)
5784: "according to the number of the people of Israel" (Masoretic Text), with a footnote on the alternative
5786: "according to the number of the angels of God" (some manuscripts: "sons of God")
5787: Most textual critics, including many conservative ones, now think "sons of God" is the older reading and "sons of Israel" a later change. Three reasons are usually given. First, the oldest witnesses (the Qumran scroll and the Greek) agree against the medieval text. Second, "sons of Israel" fits awkwardly: Israel did not yet exist when the nations were divided (Gen 10–11), and verse 9 sets Israel apart as Yahweh's own portion, distinct from the other nations. Third, a scribe is more likely to have changed "sons of God" to "sons of Israel" (to avoid a reading that seemed to give other gods authority over the nations) than the other way round. Defenders of the Masoretic reading reply that Jewish tradition linked the seventy nations of Gen 10 to the seventy people of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:27; Exod 1:5; Deut 10:22), so "sons of Israel" makes sense in its own way; and that some versions and commentators keep the received text out of respect for it, while noting the alternative.
5788: With "sons of God", the verse says that when the nations were divided (most connect this with Babel, Gen 11), God set their boundaries according to the number of heavenly beings, while keeping Israel for himself (Deut 32:9). Read with Deut 4:19-20 and Deut 29:26, where the nations' worship of the "host of heaven" seems to be allotted or permitted, and Dan 10:13, 20-21, where "princes" of Persia and Greece oppose Michael, this becomes the backbone of the divine-council reading: the nations were handed over to lesser powers, who then became corrupt (Ps 82), and the gospel reclaims them. Scholars who accept the text-critical point do not all accept that whole theology: some read the verse simply as saying God's ordering of the world matches the structure of his heavenly court, without saying those beings rule the nations; others note that Deut 4:19 can mean God allowed, rather than appointed, the nations' star-worship.
